questions.question: Which is the correct way to declare a pointer?
questions.explanation: The asterisk binds to the name, so int *ptr; declares ptr as a pointer to int. int_ptr x and *int ptr are not valid declarations in C.

questions.question: If p is an integer pointer with a value 1000, then what will the value of p + 5 be?
questions.explanation: Pointer arithmetic scales by the size of the pointed type: p + 5 adds 5 × 2 = 10 bytes for a 2-byte int, giving 1010. With 4-byte ints the answer would be 1020.

questions.question: *(&num) is equivalent to writing -
questions.explanation: &num yields the address of num, and * dereferences that address straight back, so *(&num) is simply num. The two operators cancel each other.

questions.question: Address stored in the pointer variable is of type -
questions.explanation: A pointer holds a memory address, which is an unsigned integral value internally; that is why pointer arithmetic and casts to integer types are possible.
Evaluating right to left: (*ptr)-- yields 5 and makes num 4, x+2 yields 7, and ++num makes num 5 and yields 5. Printed left to right the output is 5 7 5.

questions.question: If arr is an array of integers, the arr[i] is equivalent to
questions.explanation: arr[i] is defined as *(arr + i): the array name decays to a pointer to arr[0] and the offset selects the element. The two notations are interchangeable.

questions.question: If P and Q are properly declared and initialized pointer and x, y and z are integer variables, then which of the following statement is NOT valid?
questions.explanation: *P is an int lvalue while P + 10 is an address, so *P = P + 10 assigns a pointer to an int without a cast and is invalid. The other three are legal expressions.
A union shares one storage area among all members, so its size equals the largest member. Here float needs 4 bytes, more than int (2) and char (1).

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT determined by the storage class of a variable?

options.A: The place where the variable allocates its space.
options.C: The range of values of the variable.
options.D: The initial value of the variable.

questions.explanation: A storage class fixes where the object lives, its scope, lifetime and default initial value. The range of values depends on the data type, not on the storage class.
ptr points at arr[4] and ptr - i steps backwards, so the loop prints 5, 4, 3, 2, 1. It never reads arr[-1] because i stops at 4.

questions.question: Which is false about variables and pointers?

options.A: A variable defined once can be defined again with different scope.
options.B: A single variable cannot be defined with two different types in the same scope.
options.C: A variable must be declared and defined at the same time.
options.D: A variable refers to a location in memory.

questions.explanation: Declaration and definition can be separate: extern int x; declares x while the definition lives in another file. So it is false that both must happen together.

questions.question: A structure can be placed within another structure is known as -
questions.explanation: A structure that has another structure type as a member is called nested. A self-referential structure instead contains a pointer to its own type.

What is a NULL pointer in C?

options.A: A pointer that points to the first element of an array
options.B: A pointer that points to nothing (address 0)
options.C: A pointer that stores a garbage value
options.D: A pointer that points to itself

questions.explanation: A NULL pointer holds the address 0 and deliberately points to no object, which is handy for signalling 'nothing yet'. Dereferencing it is undefined behaviour.

questions.question: What is a void pointer (generic pointer) in C?

options.A: A pointer that can only point to void functions
options.B: A pointer that can point to any data type
options.D: A pointer that always has NULL value

questions.explanation: void * is a generic pointer that can hold any object address, but it must be cast back to a real type before dereferencing because its target size is unknown.

questions.question: What does 'const int *ptr' mean?

options.A: ptr is a constant pointer that cannot change the address it holds
options.B: ptr is a pointer to a constant integer — the value pointed to cannot be changed through ptr
options.C: Both the pointer and the value are constant
options.D: ptr cannot be used at all

questions.explanation: const int *ptr makes the pointed-to int read-only through ptr, while ptr itself may be reassigned. int * const ptr would be the opposite arrangement.

questions.question: How is a pointer to a pointer declared in C?
questions.explanation: `int **ptr` declares a pointer whose target is itself an int pointer, giving two levels of indirection. C has no reference operator, so `int &ptr` is invalid.

questions.question: What is the key difference between malloc() and calloc()?

options.A: malloc() allocates memory on stack, calloc() on heap
options.B: malloc() initializes memory to zero, calloc() does not
options.C: calloc() initializes memory to zero, malloc() leaves it with garbage values
options.D: There is no difference between them

questions.explanation: calloc multiplies count by size and zero-fills the block, whereas malloc returns uninitialised memory holding garbage. Both allocate on the heap.

questions.question: What does realloc() do in C?

options.B: Allocates new memory without freeing old memory
options.C: Resizes a previously allocated memory block

questions.explanation: realloc grows or shrinks an existing heap block, copying the contents if it must move them, and returns the new address. free is still needed afterwards.

questions.question: What happens if dynamically allocated memory is not freed using free()?

options.D: The memory is freed when the function returns

questions.explanation: Heap memory is never reclaimed automatically, so an unfreed block stays reserved for the life of the process. Repeated leaks can exhaust available memory.

questions.question: What does char *str = "Hello"; create?

options.A: A character array that can be modified
options.B: A pointer to a string literal stored in read-only memory
options.C: A copy of the string on the heap

questions.explanation: The literal sits in read-only storage and str is only a pointer to it, so writing through str is undefined behaviour. char str[] = "Hello"; would make a modifiable copy.

questions.question: Which of the following correctly declares an array of 5 integer pointers?
questions.explanation: int *arr[5]; is an array of five int pointers because the subscript binds tighter than the star. int (*arr)[5] would be one pointer to an array of five ints.

questions.question: If two pointers p1 and p2 point to elements of the same array, what does p2 - p1 give?

options.C: Sum of the values pointed to

questions.explanation: Subtracting two pointers into the same array gives the number of elements between them, not the byte difference, because the compiler divides by sizeof(element).

questions.question: Which header file is required for using malloc(), calloc(), realloc() and free()?
questions.explanation: malloc, calloc, realloc and free are all declared in stdlib.h, so that header must be included. Without it the compiler lacks their prototypes.

questions.question: What is the relationship between an array name and a pointer in C?

options.A: Array name is a variable pointer that can be reassigned
options.B: Array name acts as a constant pointer to the first element
options.C: Array name and pointers are completely unrelated
options.D: Array name stores the last element's address

questions.explanation: An array name converts to a constant pointer to its first element, which is why arr[i] works, but arr = other; is illegal because the name cannot be reassigned.
